status_summary: No statutory or Board action limiting the Fed's lender-of-last-resort role or its last-resort lending has been taken. One introduced bill points toward the recommendation in part: S. 1646, the Rein in the Federal Reserve Act, introduced 2025-05-07 and referred to the Senate Banking Committee with no further action, would require public reports to Congress, updated at least every 90 days, on each quantitative easing or tightening program and each emergency lending program under section 13 of the Federal Reserve Act, with a plan to end each program within 3 years, a bar on running any such program more than one year without authorization from Congress, and congressional disapproval procedures for each report; it does not address the discount window. Other activity points the other way but is not a limit or an expansion of lending authority: S. 4585, the Discount Window Preparedness Act, introduced 2026-05-20 and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, would require larger banks to test-borrow from the discount window, direct the Board to modernize discount window operations and study ways to reduce stigma, and sets no cap on advances. In remarks of 2026-09-22 the Fed's Vice Chair reported that Reserve Banks had streamlined the Borrower-in-Custody collateral program in September 2026 and described primary credit as offered on a no-questions-asked basis; no limit on lending was announced.

timeline.event: S. 1646, the Rein in the Federal Reserve Act, was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Banking Committee; it would require public reports on each Federal Reserve emergency lending program under section 13 and bar a program from running more than one year without authorization from Congress.

S. 4585, the Discount Window Preparedness Act, was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee; it would require discount window test borrowing by banks above 10 billion dollars in assets, direct the Board to modernize discount window operations, and require a stigma study, with no cap on advances.

The Fed's Vice Chair reported that Reserve Banks streamlined the Borrower-in-Custody collateral program in September 2026 to ease pledging of loans for discount window access; no limit on lending was announced.

title: Limit the Fed's lender-of-last-resort role and curb its last-resort lending
uncertainties: No 119th Congress bill limiting discount window lending was found; congress.gov search could not be opened, so absence is not proven. The Fed's operational changes (the Borrower-in-Custody streamlining and the Discount Window Direct portal) make existing lending easier to reach but do not widen eligibility or lending authority, so the record is not staged diverged; a reader who treats easier access as opposite to the recommendation could stage it diverged. S. 4585 is an introduced bill and not operative, so it cannot set the stage. The Borrower-in-Custody change is known from the Vice Chair's remarks; the Fed web page announcing it was not opened. The American Banker article is context only. Checked systematically on 2026-10-18: Federal Register searches, agenda and proposed-rule listings, a congress.gov and govinfo.gov bill search, the Board press release list and a news search found one introduced Senate bill (S. 1646, 2025-05-07) that would limit section 13(3) emergency lending programs to one year absent congressional authorization, with no committee action; no rule, order or enacted law limits last-resort lending. A May 2026 Board proposal to make holders of a new Payment Account ineligible for discount window credit leaves existing credit programs unchanged and does not limit the general role. Proposed at the low end was chosen because S. 1646 curbs emergency lending, one of the two last-resort channels the chapter targets, but leaves the discount window untouched and sets no phase-in; not_started is the other defensible call if a reporting duty and a time limit are read as oversight rather than a limit on the role.
